description: Quality dimensions for technical, design and planning documents and reports about existing work, derived in rubric.md for pm/plans/plan-doc-eval.md. Judge templates in templates/ render these; fixtures/ exercise each one.

measure_statuses.automatic_candidate: Computable without a judge or model (parsers, section and lexicon checks, n-gram statistics). Diagnostic only until the calibration PR shows it tracks calibrated judges on this dimension; never a quality score by itself.
measure_statuses.needs_calibration: Judge-scored or produced by a prompted model through claude-mixed. Must not drive selection until the calibration PR reports consistency, agreement and bias sensitivity for this dimension and case type.
measure_statuses.deferred: Needs inference-engine access (classifier probabilities, perplexity, NLI logits). Outside the first PRs per plan-doc-eval; listed so later work starts from the literature.

measure_readiness_values.automatic_candidate: At least one automatic_candidate quality measure exists besides the judge measure; bias covariates do not count.
measure_readiness_values.calibration_required: Only judge or model measures exist; the dimension cannot be measured at all before calibration evidence.

dimensions.name: Purpose, context and audience
dimensions.definition: The document states what problem it addresses, why now, for whom, and what decision or action it asks of the reader, and its content is selected for that reader's needs.

track_notes.continuation: The section serves the purpose the prefix has established and the role the section's position implies; re-introducing the document's purpose is scored under continuity, not here.

dimensions.derived_from: AAC&U 'context of and purpose for writing'; ISO 24495 'relevant'; PEP motivation, KEP motivation/goals, Shape Up problem and appetite, Google 'context and scope'; Grice's maxim of relation.
detection_guidance: Can a reader state the problem, the intended reader and the requested decision after the first screen?
Is there material that serves no identifiable reader need (history of the author's process, general tutorials, marketing)?
Does the document address a different problem than the brief asks for, or a generic version of it?

For reports about existing work (digests, sign-off and QA reports), can the reader tell what the report asks of them: a decision, an approval, something to watch? Whether the details carry weight in proportion to that is scored under salience_and_synthesis.
not_a_defect: A short motivation when the brief already establishes shared context.
Background that a reviewer needs to evaluate the decision.

strong.text: Because this is a summary, it does not contain all the information that may be important to you. You should read the entire proxy statement and its appendices carefully before you decide how to vote.
strong.note: The rewrite names the reader and the decision the summary serves ('before you decide how to vote').

weak.text: This Summary does not purport to be complete and is qualified in its entirety by the more detailed information contained in the Proxy Statement and the Appendices hereto, all of which should be carefully reviewed.

dimensions.judge_question: Does the document make its problem, intended reader and requested decision clear, and select content for that reader?

score_anchors.1: Purpose absent or wrong; content generic or aimed at no identifiable reader.
score_anchors.3: Purpose recoverable but late or vague; some content serves no reader need.
score_anchors.5: Problem, reader and requested decision clear early; content consistently selected for that reader.

candidate_measures.name: judge_purpose
candidate_measures.description: Rubric judge score and paired preference on this dimension.

dimensions.name: Salience and synthesis
dimensions.definition: Emphasis follows importance: what the reader most needs (the main conclusion, the decisions, the core constraints) comes early and gets the most weight, details are subordinated to the points they support, and the document pulls them together into an overview the reader can act on rather than an inventory of facts.

track_notes.continuation: Within the section: its main point is clear and its details serve it. Repeating the prefix is scored under continuity, not here.

dimensions.derived_from: SummEval 'relevance' (selection of the important content of a source); Minto's governing thought and pyramid; the Army's bottom line up front (DA PAM 600-67); GOV.UK front-loading; plain-language 'put the main point first'; Grice's maxims of quantity and relation.
detection_guidance: After the first screen, can the reader state the main conclusion and what needs their decision?
Compare space with importance: flag details that get more words than the core constraints or decisions, and core constraints mentioned once in passing.
Flag details introduced without saying what they mean for the reader (why this matters here).
Flag inventories: lists of facts, components or changes with no statement of what they add up to.
Filler and restatement are scored under concision and the order of sections under organization_and_progression; this dimension is about what gets weight and whether the parts are synthesised.
not_a_defect: Reference sections or appendices that hold detail on purpose, after the main points.
Genre-mandated order that puts background first, when the main point is still stated where readers of that genre look (abstract, summary, executive summary).

strong.text:
Abstract

This document describes the TinyMT32 Pseudo Random Number Generator (PRNG) that produces 32-bit pseudo-random unsigned integers and aims at having a simple-to-use and deterministic solution.  This PRNG is a small-sized variant of Mersenne Twister (MT) PRNG.  The main advantage of TinyMT32 over MT is the use of a small internal state, compatible with most target platforms that include embedded devices, while keeping a reasonably good randomness that represents a sigificant improvement compared to the Park-Miller Linear Congruential PRNG.  However, neither the TinyMT nor MT PRNG are meant to be used for cryptographic applications.
strong.note: An IESG reviewer said the not-for-cryptography warning was 'more buried than it should be'; the next revision put it in the abstract.

score_anchors.1: Main point and core constraints buried or missing; an inventory of details with no synthesis.
score_anchors.3: Main point findable; some core constraints underweighted or details left unconnected to what they mean.
score_anchors.5: Main point and decisions up front; weight tracks importance; details serve a clear overview.

candidate_measures.description: Rubric judge; must name the points it considers most important and where the document places them.

candidate_measures.name: lead_coverage
candidate_measures.description: Content-word recall of the brief's obligation items (for reports, of headline facts in the material such as failing tests or changed interfaces) within the first fifth of the document, compared with the reference distribution for the document kind; flags buried core constraints.

candidate_measures.name: emphasis_allocation
candidate_measures.description: A prompted model ranks the brief's or material's items by importance; words spent on each item in the document are compared with that ranking.

dimensions.name: Fidelity to brief, prefix or described material
dimensions.definition: Every claim, decision and constraint the document attributes to the brief (or, for continuations, to the prefix) is supported by it and none contradicts it; elaboration beyond the input is consistent with it and recognisable as the writer's proposal rather than presented as agreed fact. For reports about existing work, every claim about the material the report describes (code, diffs, logs, test results) is supported by that material.

track_notes.continuation: Judge against the prefix: no contradiction of decisions, names, numbers or scope established earlier in the document.

dimensions.derived_from: ISO 29148 'correct'; summarisation consistency literature (FActScore atomic claims, SummaC/FactCC entailment, QAGS question answering, SummEval 'consistency'); Grice's maxim of quality.
detection_guidance: Split the document into atomic claims; for each claim that refers to the input, check that the input supports it.
Flag numbers, names, identifiers, dates and owners that do not appear in the input and are stated as given rather than proposed.
Flag reversals: a constraint from the input stated with the opposite polarity or a weakened obligation (MUST to SHOULD).
For PM plans, flag decisions attributed to the human that the conversation shows the assistant proposed and the human did not accept.
For reports, check claims about code, tests and runs against the material: a file, function, test or result the report names must exist and do or say what the report says.
not_a_defect: Useful elaboration, reasoning or design detail that is consistent with the input, even when the input never mentions it.
Explicitly marked proposals or assumptions.

score_anchors.1: Contradicts the input on a material point or invents agreed decisions.
score_anchors.3: No material contradiction, but some unsupported specifics are stated as given.
score_anchors.5: All input-attributed content supported; elaboration consistent and clearly the writer's proposal.

candidate_measures.description: Rubric judge with the brief or prefix in view; must quote the conflicting passages.

candidate_measures.name: atomic_claim_support
candidate_measures.description: FActScore-style: a prompted model decomposes the draft into input-referring claims and labels each supported/contradicted/unsupported against the input.

candidate_measures.name: nli_consistency

candidate_measures.name: cited_artifact_resolution
candidate_measures.description: For reports, file paths, symbols, commit ids and test names the report cites resolve in the repository at the stated revision, and quoted counts or log lines appear in the material. Catches invented references, not wrong descriptions of real ones.

dimensions.name: Requirement coverage and traceability
dimensions.definition: Every requirement, constraint, scope decision and open question in the brief is carried into the document where a reader would look for it, so each can be traced back to its source.

track_notes.continuation: Coverage is measured against commitments the prefix makes for this section (announced topics, promised details, 'see section N'), not against a brief.

dimensions.derived_from: ISO 29148 and INCOSE set-level completeness; requirements traceability (Gotel and Finkelstein pre-requirements traceability); NASA requirement traceability; QAGS-style question answering adapted from summaries to briefs.
detection_guidance: List the brief's requirements, constraints, non-goals and explicit questions; locate each in the document.

A requirement is lost when it is absent, merged into a broader statement that no longer implies it, or moved to a place where the reader of that part would not find it (for PM plans: stated in the intro but absent from the PR that must implement it).
For continuations, list what the prefix promised this section would cover and check each.
not_a_defect: Requirements consolidated into one statement that still implies each.
A requirement deliberately deferred with a stated reason.

score_anchors.3: Most present; one material requirement missing, diluted or misplaced.
score_anchors.5: Every requirement traceable to an appropriate place in the document.

dimensions.name: Scope and level of abstraction
dimensions.definition: The document works at the level of detail its kind and stage call for: it fixes the decisions a reader must review now, states goals and non-goals, and leaves implementation choices that do not affect those decisions to the people who implement them.

track_notes.continuation: The section's level of detail matches the prefix's and the section's role; a reference-level section may be detailed where an overview section may not.

dimensions.derived_from: ISO 29148 and INCOSE 'appropriate' level and solution-free requirements; NASA implementation-free requirements; Google design docs ('really implementation manuals'); Shape Up 'rough, solved, bounded' (wireframes too concrete, words too abstract; no-gos as the boundary); RFC 4101 detail for implementors gets in the way of review; KEP goals/non-goals; Diátaxis separation of purposes.
detection_guidance: Mark passages that fix function names, file layouts, data-structure fields, flags or step-by-step code changes; ask whether any reviewed decision depends on them.
Premature implementation detail is detail that constrains implementers without a reason the document states, or that buries the decisions under it.
The opposite failure also counts: so abstract that no decision is made (words too abstract).
Check for explicit non-goals or boundaries.
not_a_defect: Interface, schema or protocol detail that is itself the decision under review.
Detail the brief explicitly requests.
Reference-level sections in genres that require them (PEP specification, RFC protocol detail).
In reports about existing work, file, function, test or commit references given as evidence for a claim: they locate, they do not prescribe.

strong.text:
Backwards Compatibility
=======================

This PEP changes the rules for how ``TypedDict`` behaves (allowing subclasses to
inherit from ``TypedMapping`` protocols in a way that changes the resulting
overloads), so code that inspects ``TypedDict`` types will have to change. This
is expected to mainly affect type-checkers.

The ``TypedMapping`` type will be added to the ``typing_extensions`` module,
enabling its use in older versions of Python.
strong.locator: PEP 705 Backwards Compatibility, reviewed draft (weaker) and next revision (stronger)
strong.note: The reviewer called the metaclass workaround 'a bit too much implementation detail' and asked to cut everything from 'Users wanting to inherit'.

weak.text:
Backwards Compatibility
=======================

This PEP changes the rules for how ``TypedDict`` behaves (allowing subclasses to
inherit from ``TypedMapping`` protocols in a way that changes the resulting
overloads), so code that inspects ``TypedDict`` types will have to change. This
is expected to mainly affect type-checkers.

The ``TypedMapping`` type will be added to the ``typing_extensions`` module,
enabling its use in older versions of Python. Users wanting to inherit from
both ``TypedDict`` and ``TypedMapping`` will need to use
``typing_extensions.TypedDict`` in these versions, as the existing ``typing`` implementation
of ``TypedDict`` does an ``is`` check on the metaclass of all base classes and raises
an error if any other metaclass is found. This would cause any subclass of both
that implementation and a ``TypedMapping`` protocol to trigger an error at runtime.
weak.locator: PEP 705 Backwards Compatibility, reviewed draft (weaker) and next revision (stronger)

score_anchors.5: Detail tracks the decisions; boundaries and non-goals explicit.

dimensions.name: Rationale, trade-offs and alternatives
dimensions.definition: Decisions come with the reasons for them, the trade-offs accepted and the credible alternatives rejected, so a reviewer can disagree with a specific step rather than with the whole.

track_notes.continuation: Applies when the section makes or defends decisions; a purely descriptive section is judged on whether it supports decisions made elsewhere.

dimensions.derived_from: ISO 42010 decision rationale; Rust RFC 'drawbacks' and 'rationale and alternatives'; PEP rationale and rejected ideas; Google 'alternatives considered'; KEP alternatives; NASA trade studies; AAC&U 'sources and evidence'.
detection_guidance: For each consequential decision, look for a reason tied to a goal or constraint.
Check that rejected alternatives are ones a knowledgeable reviewer would raise, and that the reason for rejection is specific.
Flag straw-man alternatives and rationale that only restates the decision.
not_a_defect: Decisions the brief already settled, cited rather than re-argued.

strong.text:
# Rationale and alternatives [rationale-and-alternatives]: #rationale-and-alternatives

We could require that multiple attributes must be within in a delimiter to make it so that it's always two arguments at the top level. E.g., `#[cfg_attr(predicate, [attr, attr])]`. While this could increase clarity, it mostly seems like it would just add noise. In the multiline case, it already reads pretty clear with the predicate on the first line and each attribute indented.

The default alternative of not doing this is a possibility. It would just mean that conditionally including attributes is slightly less ergonomic than it could be.
strong.locator: Rationale and alternatives, before and after commit ad8ba5ef
strong.note: The draft said 'There are no other alternatives'; after a reviewer raised the bracket syntax, the author added it with a reason for rejecting it.

candidate_measures.description: Rubric judge score and paired preference.

dimensions.name: Organization and progression
dimensions.definition: The document moves from context to decision to detail in an order a reader can follow: overview before specifics, terms defined before use, dependencies before what depends on them, and each part building on what came before, down to each sentence picking up from the one before it, without formatting that cuts the links between connected ideas.

track_notes.continuation: Judge order within the section; restarting the prefix, looping back over it or jumping ahead of material it has not yet introduced is scored under continuity, not here.

dimensions.derived_from: Gopen and Swan reader expectations (old before new, stress position); Williams on cohesion and coherence; Minto governing idea first; RFC 4101 model before detail; Rust RFC guide-level before reference-level; 6+1 'organization'; AAC&U 'content development'; plain-language 'organize to meet readers' needs'; GOV.UK front-loading; Coh-Metrix cohesion and the entity-grid model of local coherence; format-bias findings for the judge-side risk of rewarding lists and bold.
detection_guidance: Read only headings and first sentences: do they tell the argument in order?
Flag terms, components or PRs used before they are introduced, and conclusions that appear before the material supporting them without signposting.
Flag sections whose order would have to change for the dependencies among them to make sense (for PM plans, a PR described before the PRs it depends on without reason).
Flag repeated returns to the same topic in separate places.

Within paragraphs, check that each sentence picks up something from the one before (known information first, new information last). Flag non-sequiturs: sentences whose link to the previous one is a leap the reader has to supply.

Flag formatting that fragments reasoning: bullet lists whose items depend on each other but drop the connectives (because, so, but, which means) that would say how, and headings or bold so dense they flatten what matters.
not_a_defect: A summary-first structure that states conclusions up front by design (pyramid order).
Genre-mandated section order.
Lists of genuinely parallel items, steps or reference values.

strong.text: The compact fluorescent bulb has become the standard bulb for household lamps. Until recently, most lamps used incandescent bulbs. This type of bulb operates by heating a tungsten filament until it glows, throwing off light. Unfortunately, heating the filament wastes approximately 90% of the energy used to produce the light.
strong.note: The source says both versions contain the same information; in the stronger one each sentence opens on what the previous one ended with.

weak.text: The compact fluorescent bulb has become the standard bulb for household lamps. Until recently, most people used incandescent bulbs in their lamps. Heating a tungsten filament until it glows, throwing off light, is how this type of bulb operates. Unfortunately, approximately 90% of the energy used to produce the light is wasted by heating the filament.

dimensions.judge_question: Can a reader follow the document front to back, with context before detail, terms before use, each part building on the last and each sentence following from the one before?

score_anchors.1: Order obstructs understanding; frequent use-before-introduction, loops, non-sequiturs or fragments that leave the reader to supply the connections.
score_anchors.3: Generally ordered with some jumps, forward references, repeated returns or unconnected sentences.
score_anchors.5: Clear progression at every level; headings alone tell the argument and sentences follow from one another.

candidate_measures.name: list_fragmentation

dimensions.name: Concision and information density
dimensions.definition: Each passage adds information the reader needs; the document omits filler, restatement, obvious material and generic advice that would hold for any project, while keeping elaboration and repetition that help the reader.

track_notes.continuation: Judge filler and restatement within the section; repetition of the prefix itself is scored under continuity, not here.

dimensions.derived_from: Grice's maxim of quantity; plain-language 'omit excess words'; Williams on redundant and implied words; Microsoft 'get to the point fast'; Write the Docs ARID as the counterweight (useful repetition is allowed); verbosity-bias literature for the judge-side risk.
detection_guidance: For each paragraph ask: would a reader of this document lose anything if it were deleted?
Flag generic statements true of any project ("testing is important"), restatements of the previous paragraph, summaries of summaries, and hedging chains.
Distracting material also counts: content that draws a reviewer's attention away from the decisions that need review.
Judge density, not length: a long document can be concise and a short one padded.
not_a_defect: Useful elaboration, examples and reasoning beyond the brief.
Deliberate repetition for skimmability (a one-line summary at the top of a long section).
Length the genre requires.

dimensions.name: Clarity and precision
dimensions.definition: Statements have one reasonable reading: obligations are explicit, quantities and conditions are specific, terms are defined, and sentences are readable for the intended audience.

track_notes.continuation: Terms the section introduces are defined; renaming or redefining terms the prefix established is scored under continuity, not here.

dimensions.derived_from: ISO 29148 'unambiguous'; INCOSE rules against vague terms, escape clauses and open-ended lists; RFC 8174 requirement keywords; RFC 7322 editorial clarity; Google style; ISO 24495 'understandable'; 6+1 'word choice' and 'conventions'; AAC&U 'control of syntax and mechanics'.
detection_guidance: Flag vague qualifiers (appropriate, as needed, fast, robust, user-friendly, etc., and/or) where a reviewer needs a specific value or condition.
Flag obligations whose force is unclear (should vs must) when it matters.
Flag pronouns or 'this' with more than one plausible referent, and undefined acronyms. One concept named several ways is scored under internal_consistency, not here.

Flag shorthand from the writer's working context (internal names, ticket or PR ids, code identifiers, jargon) used as if the reader shared that context. A report for a reader who does not read the code needs each such term introduced or described in plain words.
not_a_defect: Deliberate openness that is labelled as an open question.

dimensions.name: Internal consistency
dimensions.definition: The document does not contradict itself: names, numbers, scope, decisions and dependency statements agree across sections.

track_notes.continuation: Consistency within the section and with the prefix overlaps fidelity; record contradictions of the prefix under fidelity and contradictions inside the new section here.

dimensions.name: Risks, uncertainty and open questions
dimensions.definition: The document states what could go wrong, what is unknown, and which questions remain for reviewers, instead of presenting an uncertain plan as settled. Claims carry the confidence their evidence supports, and reports about existing work say what was verified and what is inferred or assumed.

track_notes.continuation: Applies when the section's role includes risks or unresolved questions, or when it makes claims whose uncertainty the prefix has flagged.

dimensions.derived_from: KEP risks and mitigations; Rust unresolved questions; PEP open issues and security implications; Shape Up rabbit holes; RFC 3552 security considerations; Oxide RFD discussion states; Google cross-cutting concerns; ICD 203 analytic standards (express uncertainty, separate information from assumptions and judgments); Kent's words of estimative probability and the IPCC uncertainty guidance for calibrated language.
detection_guidance: Look for named risks with consequences and mitigations, not a generic 'risks: bugs may occur'.
Check that genuinely unknown things are marked as unknown. Exclusions and non-goals are scored under scope_and_abstraction, not here.
Flag false certainty: claims about performance, adoption or compatibility without evidence or caveat.

For reports, check that claims about the system's state or behaviour say how they are known (run, tested, read, inferred) where that is not obvious, and that inferences and untested assumptions are labelled. A report that sounds equally sure of everything fails here.
Flag hedges that carry no information ("should be fine", "likely") where the writer could say what was checked.
not_a_defect: A short or empty risks section for a small, low-risk change, if it says so.

strong.text:
Ordering comparisons are undefined for sentinel objects.


Backwards Compatibility
=======================

While not breaking existing code, adding a new "sentinels" stdlib module could
cause some confusion with regard to existing modules named "sentinels", and
specifically with the "sentinels" package on PyPI.

The existing "sentinels" package on PyPI [10]_ appears to be abandoned, with
the latest release being made on Aug. 2016.  Therefore, using this name for a
new stdlib module seems reasonable.

If and when this PEP is accepted, it may be worth verifying if this has indeed
been abandoned, and if so asking to transfer ownership to the CPython
maintainers to reduce the potential for confusion with the new stdlib module.


How to Teach This
=================

The normal types of documentation of new stdlib modules and features, namely
doc-strings, module docs and a section in "What's New", should suffice.


Security Implications
=====================

This proposal should have no security implications.

concerns.name: Padding
concerns.description: Obvious material, filler and text that adds no planning value; distracting material that draws a reviewer away from the decisions that need review.
concerns.boundary: Useful elaboration and genre-required length are not padding; judge density and relevance, not word count.

concerns.name: Premature implementation detail
concerns.description: Plans and designs that fix code-level choices (functions, files, fields, steps) before the decisions they serve are settled or reviewed.
concerns.boundary: Interfaces, schemas or protocols that are themselves under review, and detail the brief asks for, are not premature.

concerns.name: Poor progression
concerns.description: Order that makes the reader reconstruct the argument: details before context, use before introduction, loops back to settled topics; for continuations, restarting or skipping ahead.
concerns.boundary: Summary-first order and genre-mandated order are not failures.

concerns.name: Lost requirements
concerns.description: Requirements, constraints or decisions from the brief or conversation that are missing, diluted or misplaced in the document.
concerns.source: pm/plans/plan-doc-eval.md ("Preserve user intent, required plan fields and dependency semantics")
concerns.boundary: A requirement deliberately deferred with a stated reason is not lost.

concerns.name: Fidelity
concerns.description: Content attributed to the brief, prefix or described material that it does not support or that contradicts it, including assistant proposals presented as human decisions and report claims the code or runs do not bear out.
concerns.source: pm/plans/plan-doc-eval.md ("Judge factual fidelity against the brief or prefix as well as readability")
concerns.boundary: Consistent elaboration offered as the writer's proposal is not a fidelity failure.

concerns.name: Misplaced salience
concerns.description: Details that will not matter again get line after line while core constraints are mentioned briefly; no synthesis into a high-level overview the reader can steer from.
concerns.boundary: Detail placed in a reference section after the main points is not misplaced.

concerns.name: Non-sequiturs
concerns.description: Sentences that seem barely related to one another; semantic leaps that are not obvious to the reader.
concerns.boundary: A new paragraph or section that announces a change of topic is not a non-sequitur.

concerns.name: Unintroduced terms and shorthand
concerns.description: Terms, shorthand and fine details used casually without introducing them or saying why they are relevant.
concerns.boundary: Terms the intended reader already uses (from the brief or the prefix) need no introduction.

concerns.name: Unmarked uncertainty
concerns.description: Reports read as confident while the writer is guessing, and do not say what was not verified.
concerns.boundary: Plain statements of facts the material shows directly need no evidence marker.

concerns.name: Fragmenting format
concerns.description: Walls of bullets and heavy formatting in place of connected explanation.
concerns.boundary: Lists of genuinely parallel items, steps or reference values are not fragmenting.
